source: Laurence & Macedo (2023) Cognitive strategies in matrix-reasoning tasks: State of the art. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 30:147-159
finding: First review of the field. Snow (1978, 1980) proposed two strategies for multiple-choice tests. Constructive matching: study the problem, build an ideal answer, then look for it among the options. Response elimination: compare features of stem and options and discard wrong options until one is left. Bethell-Fox, Lohman and Snow (1984) tested this with eye tracking on A:B::C:D geometric analogies with four options and found constructive matching goes with higher ability. Review says almost all later work uses this paradigm because it is easy to quantify.
numbers: Bethell-Fox et al. (1984) quoted: constructive matching 'seems to involve the construction of an idealized answer which is compared to the response alternatives' (p. 207); elimination 'involves a process of feature comparison between stem and alternatives' (p. 207). The review gives no sample size for 1984.
quote: construction of an idealized answer which is compared to the response alternatives
limits: Secondary source for 1984 and 1978/1980 work; the 1984 paper is paywalled (HTTP 403) and was not opened. Review itself says most samples are university students and sample sizes are small.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact definitions to code into S3/S4: S3 builds an answer from the stem alone (no options visible); S4 compares against options. Elimination is the fallback, not a peer strategy.

source: Laurence & Macedo (2023) review, section on earlier typologies
finding: Other strategy typologies exist and overlap with Snow's. Hunt (1974): Gestalt (perceptual, extend the pattern) vs Analytic (propositional, logical operations). DeShon et al. (1995): visual strategy for easy items, verbal strategy for hard items. Kunda et al. (2010): affine vs fractal strategies from AI solvers. The review argues constructive matching/response elimination won because it is easy to measure, not because it is the only valid split.
numbers: No effect sizes. Four typologies named: Hunt 1974, DeShon 1995, Kunda 2010, Snow 1978/1980.
limits: Descriptive only. The review notes verbal (DeShon) vs response elimination may overlap.
agent_relevance: The build/check split is one of several; for an LLM the Analytic (symbolic, program-like) route is closest to constructive matching with code.

source: Vigneau, Caissie & Bors (2006) Eye-movement analysis demonstrates strategic influences on intelligence (as summarised in Rivollier et al. 2021, Table 1)
finding: Eye tracking on Raven's APM (N = 55). People who spent a larger share of time on the matrix and waited longer before first looking at the options scored higher. People who spent more time on the options and toggled between matrix and options more often scored lower. Item-level results were less clear.
numbers: Correlation with APM score (N = 55): proportional time on matrix r = .48; proportional time on alternatives r = -.44; number of toggles r = -.27; toggle rate r = -.43; latency to first toggle r = .41; absolute item latency r = .03. Mean toggles about 21; proportional time on matrix 84%; latency to first toggle 17 s (as quoted by Rivollier).
limits: Numbers read from Rivollier's comparison table, not from the 2006 paper itself. Correlations are between-person and do not prove strategy causes score. Item-level evidence weaker.
agent_relevance: Gives the measurable signature of each strategy: time before first look at options, and option-switch rate. An agent harness can log the same two things (tokens spent on the stem before the first option is cited; number of stem/option switches).

source: Rivollier, Quinton, Gonthier & Smeding (2021) Looking with the (computer) mouse. Behavior Research Methods 53:1081-1096
finding: Replicated the eye-tracking strategy indices with a mouse interface in which only the matrix or only the options is visible at a time. Strategy indices predicted APM accuracy as well as or better than eye tracking.
numbers: Experiment 1 (N = 130): proportional time on matrix r = .56; proportional time on options r = -.56; toggle rate r = -.55; latency to first toggle r = .70; total toggles r = .02 (n.s.). Reliability alpha .86 (time on matrix), .86 (latency), .92 (toggle rate). Mixed model: each extra toggle per minute cuts success by 3.5% (b = -0.14, p < .001); +10% time on matrix adds 5.8% success. Pilot N = 36; Experiment 2 N = 64.
limits: Mouse switching is costly, so toggles dropped from about 21 to 2.3 per item compared with eye tracking, yet proportional time stayed similar (76% vs 84%). Students only, mostly female. Total toggles did not predict accuracy; only the rate did.
agent_relevance: The raw count of stem/option switches is not diagnostic, but the rate per unit effort is. A trace monitor should use a rate, not a count.

source: Rivollier et al. (2021) Experiment 2: constraining option access
finding: Hiding the options for a fixed delay at the start of each item (forcing constructive matching first) raised early accuracy but the benefit reversed for people who needed longer. Evidence that forcing build-first helps only when the build can succeed.
numbers: Interaction condition x item latency b = -0.013, SE 0.006, chi2(1) = 4.80, p = .03. At the moment options appear: success .78 (Constrained, n = 29, 95% CI .62-.89) vs .65 (Unconstrained, n = 33, CI .47-.80), b = 0.66, p = .047. Benefit reverses when answers came more than 49 s after options appeared (16% of trials).
limits: Small groups; p-values near .05; the manipulation changes the task, so working memory demands may differ. Authors say strategy was manipulated only indirectly.
agent_relevance: Directly supports a rule: show options late (hide them in S3) but give a way to fall back (S4) after a budget, because a forced build with no fallback hurts on hard items.

source: Gonthier & Thomassin (2015) Strategy use fully mediates the relationship between working memory capacity and performance on Raven's matrices. JEP: General 144:916-924
finding: Experiment 1 manipulated strategy and found that when everyone was induced to use an effective strategy, the correlation between working memory capacity and Raven score fell. Experiment 2 measured strategy by a self-report questionnaire and strategy use fully mediated the working-memory to Raven link.
numbers: Experiment 1 N = 250; Experiment 2 N = 93 (abstract). Effect sizes not retrieved.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC); full text not opened. Questionnaire is self-report. Later study with a larger sample (Jastrzebski 2018) failed to replicate the mediation (see a09).
agent_relevance: Supports the view that a scaffold that imposes the right strategy can erase the gap between strong and weak solvers. This is the human version of 'a thinking schema lifts a weaker model'.

source: Gonthier & Roulin (2020) Intraindividual strategy shifts in Raven's matrices, and their dependence on working memory capacity and need for cognition. JEP: General
finding: People shift from constructive matching toward response elimination as items get harder. Strategy variation predicted most of the item-to-item variance in accuracy. Only people with high working memory and high need for cognition kept building late in the test.
numbers: Two samples of 100 each (abstract). Strategy variability predicted 78% of item-to-item variance in accuracy.
limits: Abstract only. Strategy was self-reported per item. Item order is confounded with difficulty (see a12).
agent_relevance: Confirms the fallback logic: build first, drop to elimination when the load exceeds capacity. For an agent the 'capacity' is rules held at once; the schema should detect overload and switch deliberately, not drift.

source: Jarosz, Raden & Wiley (2019) Working memory capacity and strategy use on the RAPM. Intelligence 77:101387
finding: Think-aloud protocols on the APM. Strategy partly (not fully) mediated the working memory to score link. Participants used constructive matching less as items got harder. Found a third hybrid strategy, isolate-and-eliminate: find one rule, eliminate options with it, then look for the next rule.
numbers: Per Laurence & Macedo (2023): over 50% of participants used constructive matching; pure response elimination only 3%; the rest guessed or used the hybrid. Interaction of working memory x difficulty on strategy not significant.
limits: Abstract plus the secondary review only. Think-aloud may change behaviour and lowers accuracy. Coding is by hand and subjective.
agent_relevance: Isolate-and-eliminate is a useful third state: build one partial rule, use it to prune options, repeat. It fits an LLM that cannot hold all rules but can apply one rule at a time with code checks.

source: Jastrzebski, Ciechanowska & Chuderski (2018) as reported in Laurence & Macedo (2023): failed replication of strategy mediation
finding: With a bigger sample, Jastrzebski et al. did not find that strategy use mediates the working memory to fluid reasoning link. Jarosz et al. (2019) argued questionnaires measure strategy worse than think-aloud. Laurence and Macedo say it is still unclear whether the relation holds at all.
numbers: No sample size given in the review. Gonthier & Thomassin 2015: full mediation (N = 250 and 93). Jarosz et al. 2019: partial mediation. Jastrzebski 2018: none.
limits: Original paper not opened. The disagreement is partly about measurement method (questionnaire vs think-aloud vs eye tracking), and the review notes no study has correlated the methods with each other.
agent_relevance: Do not claim 'strategy explains ability'. The safe claim is: strategy is related to accuracy and can be manipulated. Treat mediation as unsettled.

source: Mitchum & Kelley (2010) Solve the problem first: constructive solution strategies can influence the accuracy of retrospective confidence judgments. JEP: LMC 36:699-710
finding: Spontaneous constructive matching on nonverbal spatial reasoning problems went with better confidence calibration and resolution than response elimination. Requiring constructive matching (Experiment 2) improved monitoring.
numbers: Two experiments (abstract). Sample sizes and calibration statistics not retrieved.
limits: Abstract only. Per Laurence & Macedo the forced version hid the options until a keypress and did not allow going back.
agent_relevance: Building an answer first gives a concrete object to check, so confidence is more trustworthy. Fits guardrail G3: a self-built answer can be tested against the options, giving a real signal rather than a feeling.

source: Arendasy & Sommer (2013) Reducing response elimination strategies enhances the construct validity of figural matrices. Intelligence 41:234-243; Becker et al. (2016) J. Intell. 4:2 (as summarised in Laurence & Macedo 2023 and Srivastava 2023)
finding: Changing the answer format so options are harder to use for elimination raised construct validity. Becker et al. (2016) removed distractors entirely: people compose the answer from given elements, which blocks elimination and raised convergent validity. Open Matrices Item Bank now offers 220 construction-based items.
numbers: Open Matrices Item Bank: 220 items (Srivastava et al. 2023 text). Validity coefficients not retrieved.
limits: Both originals not opened; claims come from two open secondary texts. Construction format also removes the 1-in-8 guessing floor, so part of the validity gain may come from less guessing.
agent_relevance: A free-answer (no options) format is the cleanest way to force constructive matching in an LLM; in S3 the agent should commit to a generated answer before seeing any option.

source: von Gugelberg (2025) Individual Differences in Strategy and the Item-Position Effect in Reasoning Ability Measures. J. Intell. 13:77
finding: Eye tracking on APM (N = 210). Higher reasoning ability went with more constructive matching on all three metrics. The expected drift toward elimination later in the test was only partly found: toggle rate fell and time on matrix rose (more building), while time to first look at options came earlier (more eliminating). Change in strategy was linked to the item-position effect, not to reasoning ability.
numbers: N = 210 with complete eye data; n = 164 finished all 36 items; mean score 20.65 (SD 7.49); omega .91; mean total time 16.38 min of 30; toggle rate and time-on-matrix omega .97.
quote: change in strategy use was correlated with the item-position effect and not reasoning ability
limits: Strict 30-minute limit; later items affected by running out of time. Metrics disagree, so the 'shift to elimination' claim depends on which metric is used. This partly contradicts Gonthier & Roulin (2020), who used self-report.
agent_relevance: The cleanest known 'failed replication' for the fallback story. Do not hard-code that difficulty always means elimination; trigger the switch on a measured signal, not on item position.

source: von Gugelberg (2026) Individual Differences in Problem-Solving Behavior in Reasoning Tests: The Role of Item Difficulty and Item Position. J. Intell. 14:206
finding: Eye movements from 300 participants on a figural matrices test, analysed with Bayesian multilevel models. Higher reasoning ability was consistently linked to constructive matching (lower toggle rate, higher time on matrix, later first look at options) and to stronger adaptation to changing demands. Item position produced larger between-person variation than item difficulty did.
numbers: N = 300; three indices (toggle rate, proportional time on matrix, proportional time to first fixation on options). Visuospatial working memory effects were selective, not a consistent main effect.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read in detail. Observational.
agent_relevance: People differ more in how their strategy changes across a test than in how they react to difficulty. For an agent, state carried across items (fatigue-like context drift) may matter more than item difficulty.

source: Liu, He, Man & Zhan (2025) Exploring Critical Eye-Tracking Metrics for Identifying Cognitive Strategies in Raven's APM. J. Intell. 13:14
finding: Data-driven test of which eye metrics best classify strategy. Random forest with feature elimination on 7 features: proportional time on matrix (PTM) was most important, then rate of latency to first toggle (RLT) and latency to first toggle (LFT). Clustering on these three found two clusters on 27 of 36 items; cluster 1 (more matrix time, later first toggle) was smaller and had higher accuracy. Paper writes a mixture model: P(correct) is higher or equal under constructive matching, with a gain term e_j >= 0 per item, and strategy choice is a logistic function of the three metrics.
numbers: 36 APM items; 2-cluster solution optimal for 27 items, 4 clusters for 5 items; cluster 1 had higher PTM, LFT, RLT and higher accuracy (t values reported, exact N not extracted).
limits: Sample size not extracted from the text read. Clustering is unsupervised; labels 'constructive' and 'elimination' are inferred from priors, not verified by verbal report. Includes a third isolate-and-eliminate class in a 3-class variant.
agent_relevance: The formal model is directly usable: P(correct | build) >= P(correct | eliminate) with a per-item gain term, and a strategy-selection model driven by observable features. An agent could log PTM-like and LFT-like features to decide which state it is in.

source: Hayes, Petrov & Sederberg (2011) A novel method for analyzing sequential eye movements reveals strategic influence on Raven's APM. J. Vision 11(10):10
finding: A scanpath successor-representation method found two principal components of scanning patterns that predicted Raven scores much better than first-order statistics. Components were interpretable as strategic processing.
numbers: Not retrieved (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only; page returned 403. Per Laurence & Macedo, the matrix time distribution index (MTDI) was not a good predictor in Hayes 2011 and Laurence 2018.
agent_relevance: Order of looks matters, not only totals. For an agent: the sequence stem-rules -> constructed answer -> option check is a stronger marker than counts.

source: Hayes, Petrov & Sederberg (2015) as summarised in Laurence & Macedo (2023): training and strategy
finding: After practice or training on Raven, score gains were partly due to a change in strategy. Loesche, Wiley & Hasselhorn (2015) found that people taught the rules spent more time on the matrix and used constructive matching.
numbers: Strategy change accounts for about one-third of the training gain (Hayes 2015, as quoted in the review).
limits: Second-hand; originals not opened. 'One third' is a single estimate.
agent_relevance: Rules taught up front push people to build. In the schema, giving the model the catalogue of rule types (constant, progression, distribute-three, arithmetic) before it sees options should have the same effect.

source: Srivastava, Jaarsveld & Sangani (2023) Verbal-analytical rather than visuo-spatial Raven's puzzle solving favors Raven's-like puzzle generation. Front. Psychol. 14:1205056
finding: Eye tracking by puzzle type. Verbal-analytical puzzles took longer and showed more progressive/regressive saccades, read as more response elimination; also tied to ability to generate Raven-like puzzles. Text restates that constructive matching goes with higher scores and higher g-saturation, and that construction-based items have been built over the last 15 years to block elimination.
numbers: Sample size not extracted. Reports longer completion time and higher saccade counts for verbal-analytical puzzles.
limits: Interpretation of saccade counts as elimination is inferred. Boundary: representation type (visual vs verbal) changes which strategy appears.
agent_relevance: Task type matters: puzzles that must be verbalised push toward elimination. For an LLM everything is verbal, which may bias it toward elimination unless build-first is enforced.

source: Laurence et al. (2023) Eye Gaze Patterns during Reasoning Provide Insights Regarding Individual Differences in Underlying Cognitive Abilities. J. Intell. 11:75
finding: Two studies. LASSO on eye-gaze metrics from a matrices task predicted a different fluid reasoning test and other abilities. Gaze metrics from one task carried across tasks.
numbers: Gaze metrics predicted 57% of variance in fluid reasoning scores, 17% in planning, 18% in working memory.
limits: Sample sizes not extracted. Feature selection by LASSO on small samples can overfit.
agent_relevance: Strategy signatures are trait-like and portable, which supports using a trace-level strategy monitor across tasks.

source: Weber et al. (2023) A Log File Analysis on the Validity of Partial Solutions in Figural Matrices Tests. J. Intell. 11:37
finding: Construction-based matrices (people assemble the answer from parts) allow partial credit. Higher partial scores went with more structured response behaviour (fewer rule jumps) and predicted GPA better than all-or-nothing scoring, especially at lower ability.
numbers: Study 1 n = 198; Study 2 n = 169.
limits: Partial-credit advantage was mainly at lower ability. GPA criterion only.
agent_relevance: For an agent, scoring a built answer by rules satisfied (partial credit per rule) gives a graded check that elimination cannot give.

source: Zhang, Gao, Jia, Zhu & Zhu (2019) RAVEN: A Dataset for Relational and Analogical Visual rEasoNing. CVPR
finding: Built a 70,000-problem Raven-style dataset from a grammar, with human and solver baselines. Answer options were made by changing one attribute of the correct answer at a time, which later turned out to leak the answer.
numbers: Human accuracy about 84.4% overall (Table 2); heuristic solver with symbolic access 100% in several configurations; LSTM about 13%, CNN about 37%, ResNet 53.4% (Hu 2021 re-run) before the structure-aware DRT add-on.
limits: Option-generation flaw (see a21). Human sample: college students, 'simple familiarisation' only.
agent_relevance: A benchmark where the answer set is biased rewards elimination-like shortcuts. Any ARC/RAVEN-style eval we run must check for choice-only leakage.

source: Hu, Ma, Liu, Zhou, Wu, Zhou & Zhang (2021) Stratified Rule-Aware Network for Abstract Visual Reasoning (I-RAVEN). AAAI
finding: In RAVEN the right answer is the option sharing the most attributes with all others, so a model can pick it without seeing the matrix. This is machine response elimination at its purest. I-RAVEN fixes it with an attribute bisection tree. Context-blind models fall to chance.
numbers: RAVEN: ResNet 53.4%, CoPINet 91.4%, context-blind ResNet 71.9%, context-blind CoPINet 94.2% (context-blind beats the normal models). I-RAVEN: ResNet 40.3%, CoPINet 46.1%, context-blind ResNet 12.2%, context-blind CoPINet 14.2% (chance = 12.5%). SRAN 60.8% on I-RAVEN vs 60.7% on RAVEN.
quote: the correct answer can be found without the context
limits: Image-based models, not LLMs. 'Context-blind' training means the model learned the option statistics.
agent_relevance: Strongest AI evidence that choosing among options can work with zero understanding. Hence a pass obtained by elimination is weak evidence (G3): require the answer to be reproducible from the stem alone.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models. Nature Human Behaviour
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003, zero-shot) matched or beat undergraduates on a text 'Digit Matrices' task built with the rule structure of Raven's SPM. Tested both generative answers (build) and multiple-choice scored by log probability (compare options). Difficulty pattern mirrored people: more rules and progression rules were harder, spatially permuted logic problems harder than aligned ones.
numbers: Humans N = 40 (Digit Matrices); N = 80 on original image SPM with very similar error rates; GPT-3 run on 40 problems x 32 subtypes. Letter-string humans N = 57. Exact accuracies are in figures, not text.
limits: Digit format removes visual parsing. The 2023 model is old; later work (Haznitrama 2026, a28) shows image versions are much worse. Generative and multiple-choice scoring are both reported, but no direct strategy analysis.
agent_relevance: Shows both modes exist for LLMs: generative = constructive, MC log-prob = comparing options. Gives a clean experimental split for our own S3 vs S4 test.

source: Ahrabian et al. (2024) The Curious Case of Nonverbal Abstract Reasoning with Multi-Modal LLMs. COLM
finding: Tested open- and closed-source multimodal models on RPM-style items with an explicit reasoning check. Open-source models were near zero on joint answer-and-reasoning correctness; GPT-4V was far ahead. Chain-of-thought lifted closed models by up to 100%. Sample-specific hints hurt; interactive corrective hints helped.
numbers: Few-shot CoT boosted GPT-4V performance 'as much as 100%' (relative). Hints given up front were detrimental; corrective feedback gave a significant boost (figures).
limits: Dataset (IQ50) is small, 50 items. Accuracies are in figures, so exact values not quoted.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: revising from real feedback helps, while static pre-hints do not.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) How Far Are We from Intelligent Visual Deductive Reasoning? (Apple) COLM
finding: VLMs including GPT-4V and Gemini Pro scored near chance on Mensa, IntelligenceTest and RAVEN. The authors saw GPT-4V use the options together with the grid to form and test hypotheses, and sometimes eliminate options by a feature. Giving an oracle rationale did not help: hypothesis generation and verification stayed weak. Main failure was perception of confounding patterns.
numbers: Models rank in the 2-8th percentile of humans on the Mensa tests; best accuracy on IntelligenceTest 18% (Gemini Pro) against human per-question rates of 30-93.4%; humans 84.67% on RAVEN vs VLMs near chance; averages over 10 repetitions.
quote: they often use the answer options along with the grid to form and tests hypotheses
limits: Perception bottleneck confounds reasoning strategy. The observation of strategy is from a few transcripts, not a coded sample.
agent_relevance: The only study found that names model behaviour in these terms: it is mixed, not purely build-first. Evidence that unforced models drift to options-in-the-loop and elimination.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty? (IBM Research)
finding: Reasoning models fail when the problem gets longer and noisier, even with more thinking. A neuro-symbolic abductive solver (ARLC), which infers rules and builds the answer, stays robust.
numbers: o3-mini: 86.6% on I-RAVEN to 17.0% on I-RAVEN-X (near chance) with 3.4x more reasoning tokens. DeepSeek R1: 80.6% to 23.2%. ARLC: 98.6% to 88.0%.
limits: Symbolic attribute inputs with injected noise, not images. ARLC is trained/designed for the task. Authors do not code strategies.
agent_relevance: A rule-induction-then-generate program survives where free reasoning collapses: argues for code-checked rule building (S3) as the backbone rather than longer chains of thought.

source: Haznitrama, Ardi & Oh (2026) A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities (NeuroCognition). arXiv 2603.02540
finding: Same Raven-style text items given in multiple-choice and in generative (free-form) format to 10 reasoning models. Accuracy swung in different directions per model. Authors read this as: multiple choice rewards quick elimination, generative lets the model build from its internal rule representation. Human pilot found text matrices harder than image ones.
numbers: RAPM text MC to Gen: GPT-5 0.540 to 0.605; Claude Sonnet 4 0.560 to 0.385; Grok 4 Fast 0.690 to 0.555. Human text pilot N = 9: MC 0.430 (SD .167), Gen 0.444 (SD .183); human image accuracy 0.814 (from Zhang 2019). Text n = 200, image n = 140 items; single run each.
quote: MC gives a small set of choices and rewards quick elimination in trade of distraction
limits: Small human pilot; single run per model; the elimination explanation is the authors' reading, not tested. Reasoning disabled for Claude and Grok because of overthinking. Format effect has mixed sign across models.
agent_relevance: The most direct measurement we found of the build vs eliminate split in LLMs: no consistent winner. Means we must test our own model on both formats before assuming build-first helps.

source: Balepur, Ravichander & Rudinger (2024) Artifacts or Abduction: How Do LLMs Answer Multiple-Choice Questions Without the Question? ACL
finding: LLMs answer multiple-choice items above the majority baseline using only the options. Memorization does not explain it; options' joint pattern matters; models can sometimes infer the missing question. This is machine response elimination on text benchmarks.
numbers: Choices-only beat majority baseline in 11 of 12 model-dataset cases (4 LLMs x ARC, MMLU, HellaSwag), gain up to 0.33 (LLaMA on HellaSwag); few-shot of 5 (MMLU) to 25 (ARC) examples; Falcon/Phi/Mixtral AQI beat choices-only on HellaSwag.
limits: Open 2023-era models; knowledge items, not matrices. Group-dynamics explanation is inferred.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready control: run our agent with the stem hidden. If accuracy beats chance, the benchmark and the agent's S4 path are leaking.

source: Balepur, Desai & Rudinger (2025) Test-Time Reasoners Are Strategic Multiple-Choice Test-Takers. arXiv 2510.07761
finding: 12 reasoning LLMs (Gemini 2.5, GPT-5/4.1, Claude, Command, DeepSeek, Qwen3) on 1000 MCQs each from ARC, MMLU, SuperGPQA, with and without the question. Reasoning helps in full MCQA more than in choices-only. Reasoning traces in choices-only mode mostly infer the question or list properties of options; shallow cue use was less common but predicted failure.
numbers: Test-time reasoning improved full accuracy in 25 of 36 model-dataset settings (text in intro says 27) and choices-only in 15 of 36. GPT-5 choices-only on ARC 0.557. Longer reasoning only slightly raises choices-only accuracy. Five coded strategies incl. ELIMINATE, INFER_Q, SHALLOW; only SHALLOW and inconsistency predicted failure (logistic regression).
limits: Single run, temperature 1.0; strategies coded on 180 traces by 2 authors; knowledge MCQs, not matrices; paper has an internal inconsistency (25 vs 27).
agent_relevance: Elimination in a trace is not by itself a failure signal: ELIMINATE did not predict failure, SHALLOW did. A monitor should flag shallow cue use, not all elimination.

source: Li (2025) A Study of Rule Omission in Raven's Progressive Matrices. arXiv 2510.03127
finding: Trained models on I-RAVEN with one or two rules removed from training, tested on the removed rules. Text-encoded transformers and CoPINet/DCNet were compared. Per-token accuracy stayed high while choosing the correct option was much lower, showing attribute-level fit without rule-level understanding.
numbers: Seq2seq transformer remove-one-rule: per-token accuracy 96.9% (Center), 71.9% (2x2), 66.3% (3x3) but correct-choice accuracy 45.3%, 49.8%, 44.7%.
limits: Small, single-author study; models trained from scratch, not prompted LLMs. Only a subset of numbers read.
agent_relevance: Getting attributes right is not the same as having the rule. Another reason to check the built answer by applying the rule to a held-out row (G3).

source: Rivollier et al. (2021) and Vigneau et al. (2006): validity of strategy indices as proxies
finding: Authors flag open problems: the indices are assumed, not proven, to track the two strategies; alternation depends on the interface; and in a version where options hide the matrix, working memory demand may differ. Kucharsky et al. (2020), cited in Laurence & Macedo, clustered eye movements without prior labels and found row-wise vs column-wise scanning, not an elimination pattern.
numbers: No new numbers. Kucharsky 2020 clustering found constructive-like patterns plus a mixed row/column pattern; Laurence & Macedo suggest it may be a 'frustrated constructive matching' rather than pure elimination.
limits: Kucharsky paper not opened; read only through the review. Competing explanation: pure response elimination may be rarer than assumed (Jarosz: 3% pure).
agent_relevance: Warns against a two-state model: real solving mixes building and checking. The schema should allow S3 and S4 to alternate under code control, not be exclusive modes.
